scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

Let me break this down step by step. First, I need to understand the situation fully. My brother has Asperger's, which is a form of autism. He's extremely smart, excels in math and physics, and is doing well in college. However, he's been struggling with depression, to the point where he attempted suicide a few months ago. He's in outpatient treatment now. The family knows about his diagnosis, but it's not something we talk about openly because he's embarrassed by it. I'm very close to him, and he only talks to me about these things. Recently, a nurse at the hospital asked me if my brother had ever been diagnosed with autism because she noticed some signs. I talked to my brother about it today, and he's still denying that he has autism. He loves me a lot, and I love him just as much. We've always been close, and as we've gotten older, we've become more alike, which he seems to really enjoy. I've tried talking to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed of it. I've mentioned that some famous people like Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs are thought to have Asperger's, but that doesn't seem to help him. I'm considering telling him that I have Asperger's too, thinking that it might help him accept his own diagnosis and not feel so alone. But I'm wondering if that's a good idea or if it's wrong to lie to him like that. So, is it right or wrong to lie to my brother about having a disorder to make him feel better and help him move forward? Let's think about the possible consequences of this action. On one hand, lying could make him feel less alone. If he thinks I have the same disorder, he might be more open to accepting his own diagnosis and seeking help. It could strengthen our bond, and he might feel more supported knowing that I understand his struggles firsthand. On the other hand, lying could damage our trust. If he finds out that I lied to him, he might feel betrayed, and our relationship could suffer. It could also send the wrong message about the importance of honesty, especially in our family where trust is crucial. Another thing to consider is the potential impact on my brother's self-esteem and mental health. If he starts to rely on the lie to feel better about himself, it might prevent him from addressing his real issues and seeking appropriate help. It could also delay his acceptance of his diagnosis, which is important for his long-term well-being. I also need to think about the ethical implications of lying. Generally, honesty is valued because it builds trust and fosters healthy relationships. Lying, even with good intentions, can have negative consequences that aren't immediately apparent. Perhaps instead of lying, I could find other ways to support him. I could encourage him to talk about his feelings, provide resources about Asperger's, or help him connect with others who have similar experiences. Building his self-esteem and helping him see his strengths might be more effective than trying to make him feel less alone by lying. I also wonder if there's a middle ground. Maybe I could share some of my own experiences with challenges or differences, without necessarily lying about having the same disorder. That way, I can still show him that he's not alone without compromising the truth. It's also important to consider the long-term effects of this decision. If I lie to him now, how will that affect our relationship in the future? Will it cause more problems down the line, especially if he ever finds out the truth? In summary, while the intention behind lying might be to support my brother and help him feel less alone, the potential negative consequences, such as damaged trust and delayed acceptance of his diagnosis, seem significant. It might be better to approach the situation with honesty and find other ways to support him without resorting to deception.
